metadata.title: An algebraic approach to virtual fundamental cycles on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves

extraction_notes.note: Theorems B.1.1, 9.2.13, 10.3.12 and Propositions 10.3.10/10.6.21 are proved in running text spread over many subsections and whole appendices (B, C) with no proof environment; rather than one appendix-long proof node, each concluding argument is its own proof part with proves edges, and the lemmas/definitions of the appendices are separate nodes.
The introduction's Poincare duality argument is a sketch of Lemma A.6.63; given alternative:true on its proves edge but no rigor field, since rigor is not allowed on proof nodes.
The same ground-ring convention environment is repeated verbatim at the start of Sections 4, 5 and 6; each is kept as its own node since each is scoped to its section.

The introduction and technical introduction (Sections 1-2) give informal versions of later definitions; they are separate nodes, but no term edges were drawn from them into the body, which relies on the formal definitions.
Several remark/definition environments retyped by content: F19, F84, F202, F557 are definitions; F312 (Gysin sequence, in a definition environment) is an external theorem.
F537 retyped as conjecture ('we expect') and F606 as open_problem (an unresolved question); F359 kept as remark though it states an expectation.
Results the paper calls well known or whose proofs are 'lifted from' McDuff-Salamon, Wehrheim or Floer are marked external, with their proofs kept as paper proofs.
Editorial Remark A.2.23 was dropped; the historical paragraph of 10.7 and literature surveys at the start of Appendix B and A.9 were not extracted, as cited results there are only mentioned.
Long one-sentence setups spanning lists or paragraphs (basepoint data, construction of $Q_{0,0,0}$) are single definition nodes with the term-introducing sentences inside nested as definitions.

Appendix B and C term edges were not drawn across the two appendices: Appendix C re-introduces its own $C_0$, $u_\alpha$, necks, $K$, gluing map with different meanings, so same-symbol uses there do not depend on Appendix B's definitions.

nodes.name: VFC paradigm: symplectic manifold to moduli spaces to invariant
nodes.statement: \begin{matrix}\text{Symplectic}\cr\text{manifold}\end{matrix}\;\Longrightarrow\;\begin{matrix}\text{Moduli space(s) of}\cr\text{pseudo-holomorphic curves}\end{matrix}\;\overset{\text{VFC}}\Longrightarrow\;\begin{matrix}\text{Desired}\cr\text{invariant}\end{matrix}
nodes.statement_short: Schematic: a symplectic manifold gives moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves, whose virtual fundamental cycles give invariants.
nodes.label: paradigm

nodes.name: Local chart, obstruction space, thickened moduli space, Kuranishi map
nodes.statement_short: A local chart for $X$ is $X\supseteq s_\alpha^{-1}(0)\subseteq X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$ with obstruction space $E_\alpha$, thickened moduli space $X_\alpha$ and Kuranishi map $s_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Local chart of a moduli space
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} X\ar[hookleftarrow]{r}{\text{open}}&s_\alpha^{-1}(0)\ar[hook]{r}{\text{closed}}&X_\alpha\ar{r}{s_\alpha}&E_\alpha \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: localchart

nodes.name: Regular locus
nodes.statement_short: The regular locus $X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_\alpha$ is where $X_\alpha$ is cut out transversally, a finite-dimensional manifold.
nodes.statement: For the purpose of constructing the virtual fundamental cycle of $X$, such a local chart \eqref{localchart} is useful over $X\cap X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}$, where $X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_\alpha$ (called the \emph{regular locus}) is the locus where $X_\alpha$ is cut out transversally (and thus, in particular, $X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a finite-dimensional manifold).

nodes.name: Implicit atlas (informal)
nodes.statement_short: Informally, an implicit atlas is an index set $A$ with obstruction spaces $E_\alpha$ and $I$-thickened spaces $X_I$ fitting together, with $X_\varnothing=X$.
nodes.statement: An implicit atlas is an index set $A$ (whose elements are called \emph{thickening datums}) along with obstruction spaces $E_\alpha$ (for all $\alpha\in A$) and $I$-thickened moduli spaces $X_I$ (for all finite subsets $I\subseteq A$) fitting together globally in a natural generalization of \eqref{localchart}, where \emph{the $\varnothing$-thickened moduli space $X_\varnothing$ is identified with the original moduli space $X$}.

nodes.name: Virtual dimension and $E_I$
nodes.statement_short: The virtual dimension $d$ of an implicit atlas satisfies $\dim X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}=d+\dim E_I$ with $E_I=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$.
nodes.statement: In particular, an implicit atlas carries a parameter $d\in\mathbb Z$, the \emph{virtual dimension}, and we require that $\dim X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}=d+\dim E_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$ (where $E_I:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$).

nodes.name: Implicit atlases as presentations of derived manifolds
nodes.statement: From a theoretical standpoint, it would be desirable to endow the moduli space $X$ with the canonical structure of a ``derived manifold'' (a notion which should be more intrinsic than the notion of an implicit atlas on $X$). A good notion of a ``derived smooth manifold'' exists (due to Spivak \cite{spivak}, Borisov--Noel \cite{borisovnoel}, and Joyce \cite{joyceI,joyceII}), and it is reasonable to expect that a parallel topological theory exists as well. By nature, the theory of derived manifolds uses the language of higher category theory. An implicit atlas on $X$ may be thought of as giving a ``presentation'' of $X$ as a derived manifold (just as a collection of open sets of $\mathbb R^n$ and gluing data can be used to present an ordinary manifold). The ``atlas'' approach which we follow here, while being less intrinsic, has the advantage of being more concrete and more elementary. We believe that a more intrinsic approach is unlikely to lead to any simplification in the construction of this extra structure (implicit atlas or derived manifold structure) on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. However, it would likely make it easier to work with (and, in particular, calculate) virtual fundamental cycles on such spaces.
nodes.statement_short: An implicit atlas can be viewed as a presentation of the moduli space as a derived manifold; the atlas approach is more concrete.

nodes.name: Domain stabilization
nodes.statement_short: Domain stabilization: every curve meets some codimension-two submanifold $D$ transversally so that $u^{-1}(D)$ as marked points stabilizes the domain.
nodes.statement: The first step requiring setting-specific arguments is \emph{domain stabilization}.  For any pseudo-holomorphic curve $u:C\to M$ in $X$, we must show that there is a smooth codimension two submanifold (possibly with boundary) $D\subseteq M$ which intersects it transversally such that adding $u^{-1}(D)$ as added marked points on $C$ makes $C$ stable.

nodes.name: $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$ for thickened moduli spaces
nodes.statement: For the $I$-thickened moduli spaces $X_I$, we denote by $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_I$ the locus where the relevant linearized operator is surjective.

nodes.name: Openness and submersion axioms (informal)
nodes.statement: We must show that $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is open and is a topological manifold of the correct dimension (we also need a certain topological submersion condition on how $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is cut out inside $X_J^{\mathrm{reg}}$ for $I\subseteq J$).  These are the \emph{openess and submersion axioms} of an implicit atlas.

nodes.name: Virtual cochain complex $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)$ (informal)
nodes.statement: The main object we develop is the \emph{virtual cochain complex} $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)$ defined whenever $A$ is \emph{finite}.

nodes.name: $H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}$, the map $s_\ast$ and $E_A$
nodes.statement_short: $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}$ has a canonical isomorphism $\check H^\bullet(X)\cong H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)$ and a pushforward $s_\ast$ to chains of $(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)$.

nodes.name: Fundamental isomorphism (introduction)
nodes.statement: \check H^\bullet(X)\xrightarrow\sim H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)
nodes.label: fundisointro

nodes.name: Chain-level pushforward $s_\ast$ (introduction)
nodes.statement: C^{d+\bullet}_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)\xrightarrow{s_\ast}C_{\dim E_A-\bullet}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)
nodes.label: spushforwardintro

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}_A$ (introduction)
nodes.statement_short: Composing the fundamental isomorphism with $s_\ast$ and $H_{\dim E_A}(E_A,E_A\setminus0)=\mathbb Z$ gives $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}_A\in\check H^d(X)^\vee$.
nodes.statement: Since $H_{\dim E_A}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)=\mathbb Z$, combining \eqref{fundisointro} and \eqref{spushforwardintro} yields a map $\check H^d(X)\to\mathbb Z$.  We define the virtual fundamental class to be this element $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}_A\in\check H^d(X)^\vee$; if $X$ is cut out transversally (that is, $X=X^{\mathrm{reg}}$), then it agrees with the usual fundamental class of $X$ as a closed manifold.

nodes.name: VFC from a single global chart
nodes.statement_short: For one global chart, Poincare-Lefschetz duality and $(s_\alpha)_\ast$ give $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}$, and relative chains of $X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}$ play the role of $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}$.

nodes.name: Single global chart: duality and pushforward
nodes.statement: \check H^{\dim X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}-\dim E_\alpha}(X)\xrightarrow\sim H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}},X_\alpha^{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)=\mathbb Z

nodes.name: Perturbation computes the virtual fundamental class
nodes.statement: Though our definition of the virtual fundamental cycle does not involve perturbation, we do in some sense show that perturbation is a valid way to compute the virtual fundamental class (in fact, this is an easy corollary of some of its formal properties).

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental cycles in ordinary homology only
nodes.statement: In this paper, we only construct virtual fundamental cycles in ordinary homology, which is thus inadequate for applications of moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves involving their fundamental class in smooth (or framed) bordism (e.g.\ as in Abouzaid \cite{abouzaid} or Ekholm--Smith \cite{ekholmsmith}). However, in discussions with Abouzaid, we realized that by working on the space level, one can probably upgrade our construction to yield a virtual fundamental cycle in the (Steenrod) framed bordism group of $X$, twisted by a certain ``virtual spherical normal bundle''.
nodes.statement_short: Only ordinary homology is treated; a space-level version might give classes in framed bordism twisted by a virtual spherical normal bundle.
nodes.label: smoothcandomaybe

nodes.name: Chains as a homotopy sheaf: philosophy of the VFC
nodes.statement: In broad philosophical outline, the strategy we follow to define the virtual fundamental cycle is the following. The functor $U\mapsto C_\bullet(U\operatorname{rel}\partial U)$ (or Borel--Moore chains $C_\bullet^\mathrm{BM}(U)$) is homotopy sheaf on $X$, and the virtual fundamental cycle is a global section thereof. Hence we may define the virtual fundamental cycle by \emph{specifying it on a convenient finite open cover and giving patching data on all higher overlaps} (in our case, the particular cover being $X=\bigcup_{I\subseteq A}\psi_{\varnothing I}((s_I|X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})^{-1}(0))$ for finite $A$). This philosophy is very natural and could apply quite generally.
nodes.statement_short: The virtual fundamental cycle is a global section of the homotopy sheaf $U\mapsto C_\bullet(U\operatorname{rel}\partial U)$, specified on a finite cover with patching data.
nodes.label: chainsishomotopysheaf

nodes.name: $\infty$-categories as natural setting for the VFC package
nodes.statement: The language of $\infty$-categories as developed by Lurie \cite{luriehtt} seems to be a natural setting for the VFC package and, more generally, for a good theory of derived manifolds and their virtual fundamental cycles (indeed, the existing theory of derived smooth manifolds is by necessity written in the language of higher category theory). We have avoided $\infty$-categories in this paper for sake of concreteness (though at the cost of needing to use lots of explicit homotopy colimits). However, we expect that in this more abstract framework, one could ultimately develop the most flexible calculational tools (computing virtual fundamental cycles directly from our defintion seems rather difficult, due to the inexplicit nature of the isomorphism \eqref{fundisointro}).
nodes.label: inftycategoriesbetter

nodes.name: Implicit atlas (proto version)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. A \emph{(proto) implicit atlas} of dimension $d$ on $X$ is an index set $A$ along with the following data: \begin{rlist} \item(Obstruction spaces) A finite-dimensional $\mathbb R$ vector space $E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in A$ (let $E_I:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$). \item(Thickenings) A Hausdorff space $X_I$ for all finite $I\subseteq A$, and a homeomorphism $X\to X_\varnothing$. \item(Kuranishi maps) A function $s_\alpha:X_I\to E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in I\subseteq A$ (for $I\subseteq J$, let $s_I:X_J\to E_I$ denote $\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}s_\alpha$). \item(Footprints) An open set $U_{IJ}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \item(Footprint maps) A function $\psi_{IJ}:(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)\to U_{IJ}$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \end{rlist} which must satisfy the following ``compatibility axioms'': \begin{rlist} \item$\psi_{IJ}\psi_{JK}=\psi_{IK}$ and $\psi_{II}=\operatorname{id}$. \item$s_I\psi_{IJ}=s_I$. \item$U_{IJ_1}\cap U_{IJ_2}=U_{I,J_1\cup J_2}$ and $U_{II}=X_I$. \item$\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(U_{IK})=U_{JK}\cap(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)$. \item(Homeomorphism axiom) $\psi_{IJ}$ is a homeomorphism. \setcounter{rcountsave}{\value{rcounti}} \end{rlist} and the following ``transversality axioms'': \begin{rlist} \setcounter{rcounti}{\value{rcountsave}} \item(Submersion axiom) $s_{J\setminus I}:X_J\to E_{J\setminus I}$ is locally modeled on the projection $\mathbb R^{d+\dim E_J}\to\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}$ over $0\in E_{J\setminus I}$ for $\#I\geq 1$ (in particular, taking $I=J$ implies that $X_I$ is a topological manifold dimension $d+\dim E_I$ for $\#I\geq 1$). \item(Covering axiom) $X_\varnothing=\bigcup_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq A}\psi_{\varnothing I}((s_I|X_I)^{-1}(0))$. \end{rlist}
nodes.genus: an index set $A$ along with the following data
nodes.statement_short: Simplified implicit atlas: obstruction spaces, thickenings $X_I$, Kuranishi maps, footprints and footprint maps satisfying compatibility, submersion and covering axioms.
nodes.label: IAproto

nodes.name: Basic charts
nodes.statement: Let us unpack this definition a bit.  We have manifolds $X_\alpha$ (meaning $X_I$ for $I=\{\alpha\}$) indexed by $\alpha\in A$.  Each is equipped with a function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$ and a homeomorphism $\psi_\alpha:s_\alpha^{-1}(0)\to U_\alpha$ (meaning $\psi_{\varnothing\{\alpha\}}:(s_\alpha|X_\alpha)^{-1}(0)\to U_{\varnothing\{\alpha\}}$) where $X=\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}U_\alpha$ is an open cover.  Thus so far this is nothing more than a set of charts (the ``basic charts'') of a particular form \eqref{localchart} covering $X$ and indexed by $\alpha\in A$.

nodes.name: Overlap chart $X_{\alpha\beta}$
nodes.statement: Now for every pair of basic charts $\alpha,\beta\in A$, there is a ``overlap chart'' $X_{\alpha\beta}$ with footprint $U_\alpha\cap U_\beta$ and obstruction space $E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta$.

nodes.name: Kuranishi structure charts versus implicit atlas charts
nodes.statement: The basic charts of a Kuranishi structure are indexed by the points of $X$. Hence to define a Kuranishi structure on a space $X$, one must make a choice for each $p\in X$. The charts of an implicit atlas are indexed by an abstract set $A$, and hence we can define implicit atlases without making any choices (see \S\ref{constructintro}).

nodes.name: Uniform treatment of empty and nonempty $I$
nodes.statement: Most of the axioms of an implicit atlas are stated without reference to whether $I$ is empty or nonempty. This contrasts with other approaches, where there is an axiomatic and notational distinction between the $X_I$, $\psi_{IJ}$, or $U_{IJ}$ depending on whether $I$ is empty or nonempty. We believe that our uniform treatment makes implicit atlases simpler notationally and conceptually, and this is a novel aspect of our approach.
nodes.label: Iemptynotspecial

nodes.name: Why the real definition uses $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$
nodes.statement: The requirement that $X_I$ be a manifold \emph{whenever $I$ is nonempty} is rather unnatural (c.f.\ Remark \ref{Iemptynotspecial}) and is too strong of an assumption for two different reasons. First, we do not know how to construct implicit atlases with this property on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves (it is a subtle question of choosing good neighborhoods to ensure transversality over all $X_I$ if $\#I\geq 1$). Second, with this axiom we cannot form the ``product implicit atlas'' (Definition \ref{productimplicitatlas}) which is crucial for understanding coherence of virtual fundamental cycles between moduli spaces when treating Floer-type homology theories. Thus in the real definition of an implicit atlas (Definition \ref{implicitatlasdefinition}), there is no such requirement on $X_I$. Rather, we specify open subsets $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$ (morally, this is the locus where $X_I$ is cut out transversally), and we modify the transversality axioms appropriately.
nodes.statement_short: Requiring $X_I$ to be manifolds for nonempty $I$ is too strong (no construction, no product atlas); the real definition uses open regular loci $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$.
nodes.label: bettertouseXSreg

nodes.name: Equivalence and cobordism of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: The most natural notion of ``equivalence'' between two implicit atlases $A$ and $B$ on a space $X$ seems to be the existence of a chain of inclusions of implicit atlases $A\subseteq C_1\supseteq\cdots\subseteq C_n\supseteq B$. It is common to speak of ``cobordisms'' between Kuranishi structures or Kuranishi atlases; the analogous notion of cobordism between implicit atlases (say on the same index set $A$) on a space $X$ is an implicit atlas with boundary on $X\times[0,1]$ whose restriction to the boundary coincides with the first (resp.\ second) implicit atlas on $X\times\{0\}$ (resp.\ $X\times\{1\}$). It is an easy consequence of the VFC machinery that the virtual fundamental class is invariant under both notions of equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence of implicit atlases is a zigzag of inclusions; cobordism is an implicit atlas with boundary on $X\times[0,1]$; the VFC is invariant under both.
nodes.label: equivalenceofIA

nodes.name: Covering group
nodes.statement: Fix a smooth orbifold $X$ and let $\{X_\alpha/\Gamma_\alpha=V_\alpha\subseteq X\}_{\alpha\in A}$ be an open cover, where each $X_\alpha$ is a smooth manifold with a smooth action by a finite group $\Gamma_\alpha$ (let us call this the ``covering group'').
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Overlap chart $X_I$, $\Gamma_I$ on an orbifold
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Overlap chart over an orbifold (orbifold fiber product)
nodes.statement: X_I&:=X_{\alpha_1}\underset X\times\cdots\underset X\times X_{\alpha_n}\\ \Gamma_I&:=\Gamma_{\alpha_1}\times\cdots\times\Gamma_{\alpha_n}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy
nodes.label: fpoverorbifold

nodes.name: Overlap charts are $\Gamma_I$-manifolds covering intersections
assumptions: for any finite subset $I=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\}\subseteq A$
conclusions: $X_I$ is a smooth manifold with a smooth action by $\Gamma_I$
X_I/\Gamma_I=V_{\alpha_1}\cap\cdots\cap V_{\alpha_n}\subseteq X
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Quotient of overlap chart equals intersection of chart images
nodes.statement: X_I/\Gamma_I=V_{\alpha_1}\cap\cdots\cap V_{\alpha_n}\subseteq X
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Orbifold charts form an implicit atlas
nodes.statement: As an exercise, the reader may check that this system of charts described above gives an implicit atlas in the sense of Definition \ref{implicitatlasdefinition} where every $E_\alpha=0$.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Orbifold fiber product
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y,\mathcal Z$ be orbifolds, and fix maps of orbifolds $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$. Then the \emph{orbifold fiber product} $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal Y$ is simply the categorical $2$-fiber product in the weak $2$-category of orbifolds. It exists whenever $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z$ is transverse to the diagonal $\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z$ (in particular, it exists if at least one of the maps $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$ is \emph{\'etale} as in the above example of $X_\alpha\to X$). Thurston \cite[Proof of Proposition 13.2.4]{thurston} gives an explicit hands-on definition of $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal Y$ in the case $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$ are both \'etale by working locally on $\mathcal Z$ and then gluing. In a more modern perspective (defining orbifolds as certain stacks on the site of smooth manifolds), we may define the orbifold fiber product by the following universal property: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal Y):=\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Z)}\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Y) \end{equation} for any smooth manifold $S$. The right hand side denotes the $2$-fiber product in the weak $2$-category of groupoids, which admits the explicit description: \begin{equation} G_1\times_HG_2:=\Bigl\{(g_1,g_2,\theta)\Bigm|g_1\in G_1,\,g_2\in G_2,\,\theta\!:\!f_1(g_1)\to f_2(g_2)\Bigr\} \end{equation} (with the obvious notion of isomorphism between triples $(g_1,g_2,\theta)$) for groupoids $G_1,G_2,H$ and functors $f_i:G_i\to H$. The orbifold fiber product usually does not coincide with the fiber product of the underlying topological spaces $X\times_YZ$, though there is at least always a map $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal Y\to X\times_ZY$. The construction \eqref{fpoverorbifold} would not work if we used the fiber product of topological spaces.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy
nodes.genus: the categorical $2$-fiber product in the weak $2$-category of orbifolds
nodes.statement_short: The orbifold fiber product is the 2-fiber product of orbifolds, characterized by a universal property via 2-fiber products of groupoids.
nodes.label: orbifoldfiberproductrmk

nodes.name: Universal property of the orbifold fiber product
nodes.statement: \operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal Y):=\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Z)}\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Y)
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: 2-fiber product of groupoids
nodes.statement: G_1\times_HG_2:=\Bigl\{(g_1,g_2,\theta)\Bigm|g_1\in G_1,\,g_2\in G_2,\,\theta\!:\!f_1(g_1)\to f_2(g_2)\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Setup: zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a smooth manifold $B$, a smooth vector bundle $p:E\to B$, and a smooth section $s:B\to E$ with $s^{-1}(0)$ compact.  Let us now construct an implicit atlas $A$ of dimension $d:=\dim B-\dim E$ on $X:=s^{-1}(0)$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Thickening datum for a section of a vector bundle
differentia: A smooth homomorphism of vector bundles $\lambda_\alpha:V_\alpha\times E_\alpha\to p^{-1}(V_\alpha)$.
nodes.statement:
We set $A$ to be the set of all \emph{thickening datums} where a thickening datum $\alpha$ is a triple $(V_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$ consisting of:
\begin{rlist}
\item An open set $V_\alpha\subseteq B$.
\item A finite-dimensional vector space $E_\alpha$.
\item A smooth homomorphism of vector bundles $\lambda_\alpha:V_\alpha\times E_\alpha\to p^{-1}(V_\alpha)$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Thickenings $X_I$ for a section
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Thickening $X_I$ for the zero set of a section
nodes.statement: X_I:=\Bigl\{(x,\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(x,e_\alpha)=0\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: fredholmsectionchart

nodes.name: Kuranishi maps, footprints and footprint maps for a section
nodes.statement: The function $s_\alpha:X_I\to E_\alpha$ is simply projection to the $E_\alpha$ component.  The set $U_{IJ}\subseteq X_I$ is the locus where $x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in J}V_\alpha$, and the footprint map $\psi_{IJ}$ is simply the natural map forgetting $e_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in J\setminus I$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Verify compatibility axioms for the section example
nodes.statement: It may be a good exercise for the reader to verify the compatibility axioms in this particular case.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Index set of all thickening datums is a groupoid
nodes.statement: The reader may rightfully object that the index set $A$ defined above is not a set but rather a groupoid (just as there is no ``set of all finite sets'' or ``set of all compact smooth manifolds''). There are two ways of resolving this issue. The simplest solution is to add appropriate ``rigidifying data'' to turn $A$ into a set (e.g.\ we could add the data of an isomorphism $E_\alpha\xrightarrow\sim\mathbb R^{\dim E_\alpha}$ to the definition of a thickening datum). Another (more cumbersome, and ultimately unnecessary) solution would be to just check that the notion of an implicit atlas and the accompanying theory of virtual fundamental cycles remains valid for $A$ a groupoid instead of a set (see also Remark \ref{bettertouseovercategory} for more details).
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: The class of all thickening datums is a groupoid rather than a set; fix by adding rigidifying data or allowing groupoid index sets.
nodes.label: notsetremark

nodes.name: Canonicity of the index set of all thickening datums
nodes.statement: The index set $A$ consists of \emph{all} possible thickening datums. It is thus canonical in the sense that it does not depend on any auxiliary choice. For the purposes of extracting the virtual fundamental cycle from an implicit atlas, the only choice we will need to make is that of a finite subatlas; the independence of this choice is part of the VFC machinery.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Direct sum of obstruction spaces is essential
nodes.statement: To construct the overlap charts $X_I$, it is crucial that we are able to take the abstract direct sum of the obstruction spaces $E_\alpha$. Hence, it is better to think of them as abstract vector spaces equipped with maps to $E$ over $V_\alpha$, rather than as trivialized subbundles of $E$ over $V_\alpha$ (which also imposes the unnecessary restriction that $\lambda_\alpha$ be injective), since the latter category is not closed under direct sum. To illustrate this distinction further, let us mention a problematic alternative version of \eqref{fredholmsectionchart}: \begin{equation} X_I:=\Bigl\{x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)\in\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha\Bigr)(E_I)\Bigr\} \end{equation} This definition agrees with \eqref{fredholmsectionchart} if the following map is injective: \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha:\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\to p^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigr) \end{equation} but in general it can be different, and indeed, if \eqref{lambdatotal} fails to be injective, the definition \eqref{fredholmsectionchartwrong} isn't particularly useful. Note that this can occur even if we add the requirement that each $\lambda_\alpha$ be injective. The importance of using the direct sum was independently observed by McDuff--Wehrheim \cite{mcduffwehrheim}, and it is implicit in Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{foootechnicaldetails}.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: Overlap charts need abstract direct sums of obstruction spaces; the alternative definition via images of $\lambda_\alpha$ fails without injectivity.
nodes.label: directsumisbetter

nodes.name: Problematic alternative thickening
nodes.statement: X_I:=\Bigl\{x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)\in\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha\Bigr)(E_I)\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: fredholmsectionchartwrong

nodes.name: Total obstruction map $\bigoplus\lambda_\alpha$
nodes.statement: \bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha:\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\to p^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigr)
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: lambdatotal

nodes.name: Moduli space of stable maps $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)$ (simplified setup)
nodes.statement: Specifically, we construct an implicit atlas $A$ on the moduli space of stable maps $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)$ (we fix a symplectic manifold $X$, a smooth $\omega$-tame almost complex structure $J$, and a homology class $B\in H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$).

nodes.name: Thickening datum for genus zero stable maps
nodes.statement_short: A thickening datum is $(r_\alpha,D_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$: an integer $r_\alpha>2$, a codimension-two divisor, an $S_{r_\alpha}$-module and an equivariant perturbation map.
nodes.statement:
We define $A$ to be the set of all \emph{thickening datums} where a thickening datum is a $4$-tuple $(r_\alpha,D_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$ consisting of:
\begin{rlist}
\item An integer $r_\alpha>2$; let $\Gamma_\alpha:=S_{r_\alpha}$.
\item A smooth compact codimension two submanifold $D_\alpha\subseteq X$ with boundary.
\item A finite-dimensional $\mathbb R[S_{r_\alpha}]$-module $E_\alpha$.
\item A $S_{r_\alpha}$-equivariant map $\lambda_\alpha:E_\alpha\to C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}\times X,\Omega^{0,1}_{\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}/\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,r_\alpha}}\otimes_{\mathbb C} TX)$ (where $\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,r_\alpha}$ is the universal family over the Deligne--Mumford moduli space) supported away from the nodes and marked points of the fibers.

nodes.name: Thickened moduli space $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$: maps transverse to the divisors $D_\alpha$ with labelled intersections and $e_\alpha$ solving the $I$-thickened $\bar\partial$-equation.

nodes.name: $I$-thickened $\bar\partial$-equation
nodes.statement: \bar\partial u+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(e_\alpha)(\phi_\alpha,u)=0
nodes.label: thickenedintro

nodes.name: Kuranishi and footprint maps on $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$
nodes.statement: There are obvious projection maps $s_\alpha:\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I\to E_\alpha$ and forgetful maps $\psi_{IJ}:(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)\to U_{IJ}$, where $U_{IJ}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ is the locus of curves satisfying the conidition in (\ref{firstcondition}) above for all $\alpha\in J$.

nodes.name: Intrinsic definition of thickened moduli spaces
nodes.statement: The thickened moduli spaces $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ are defined as moduli spaces of solutions to the ``$I$-thickened $\bar\partial$-equation'' \eqref{thickenedintro}. With this intrinsic definition, the convenient overlap properties of the charts (the compatibility axioms) follow rather trivially. The atlas also clearly does not depend on any choice of Sobolev norms or ``gluing profile''. On this point, it is useful to compare with other approaches, which often take the perspective of defining thickened moduli spaces as subsets of some particular Banach manifold of maps. In this context, achieving good overlap properties seems to be more difficult and less conceptual. Another inconvenience of this setting is the lack of differentiability of the reparameterization action (and large reparameterization groups for bubbles).
nodes.statement_short: Defining thickened moduli spaces by the $I$-thickened $\bar\partial$-equation makes compatibility axioms trivial and avoids choices of Sobolev norms or gluing profiles.

nodes.name: Analysis is confined to openness and submersion axioms
nodes.statement: In our approach, the most serious analytic questions are encountered in verifying the openness and submersion axioms (that is, in proving the necessary gluing theorems). We remark that these only concern the local properties of the thickened moduli spaces, and, in particular, are separated from the other technical aspects of the construction of the implicit atlas (e.g.\ the compatibility axioms, the action of the groups $\Gamma_I$, or the action of a larger symmetry group on the entire atlas).

nodes.name: Stratified smooth structure from standard gluing
nodes.statement: Standard gluing techniques suffice to verify the openness and submersion axioms for the implicit atlases we construct on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. In fact, the transition maps between gluing charts are clearly smooth when restricted to each stratum (i.e.\ for a fixed topological type of the domain), and this yields a canonical ``stratified smooth structure'' on each $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$. If one wanted to obtain a smooth structure on the $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$, one would need to construct gluing charts whose transition maps are truly smooth. This would require a choice of ``gluing profile'' (on which the resulting smooth structure would depend) and is slightly more delicate (see Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{FOOOII,foootechnicaldetails} or Hofer--Wysocki--Zehnder \cite{polyfoldGW}). Such methods might yield smooth implicit atlases (see Definition \ref{smoothIAdef}).
nodes.statement_short: Standard gluing verifies openness and submersion; it gives stratified smooth structures, while genuine smoothness would need a gluing profile.

nodes.name: Dual of \v Cech cohomology
nodes.statement: The \emph{dual of \v Cech cohomology} $\check H^\bullet(X)^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}(\check H^\bullet(X),\mathbb Z)$ is a good candidate (and it is what we choose to use, though see Remark \ref{alsogetsteenrod} for further discussion).
nodes.section: 2.3.1 What ``homology group'' does the virtual fundamental class live in?

nodes.name: Insufficiency of singular homology (Warsaw circle)
nodes.statement: Consider the Warsaw circle $W\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ as illustrated in Figure \ref{warsawfigure}; note that singular $H_1(W)=0$. Now $\mathbb R^2\setminus W$ has two connected components; let $s:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be positive on one component and negative on the other; this gives the data of an implicit atlas on $W=s^{-1}(0)$. Using any reasonable definition, we certainly want $[W]^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\check H^1(W)^\vee\cong\mathbb Z$ to be a generator, however this is clearly not in the image of singular homology under the natural map $H_\bullet(W)\to H^\bullet(W)^\vee\to\check H^\bullet(W)^\vee$. Alternatively, the pushforward of $[W]^{\mathrm{vir}}$ to a small annular neighborhood $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ of $W$ should be a generator of $H_1(A)\cong\mathbb Z$ (as one can see by perturbing $s$).
nodes.section: 2.3.1 What ``homology group'' does the virtual fundamental class live in?
nodes.statement_short: The Warsaw circle has $H_1=0$ but its virtual class should generate $\check H^1(W)^\vee\cong\mathbb Z$, so singular homology cannot house virtual classes.
nodes.label: singularhomologyisbad

nodes.name: Single-chart implicit atlas
nodes.statement: We have a space $X$, and the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of the following data.  We have a topological manifold $X_\alpha$ (not necessarily compact), a vector space $E_\alpha$, and a continuous function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$.  We also have an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)$ (see Figure \ref{implicitatlaspicture}\subref{pica}).
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.statement_short: For a single chart, the virtual class is the composite $\check H^d(X)=H_{\dim E}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)\to H_{\dim E}(E,E\setminus 0)\to\mathbb Z$.
nodes.statement:
We define the virtual fundamental class via the following diagram, which we explain below:
\begin{equation} \check H^d(X)=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}\mathbb Z
\end{equation}
(recall that $\dim X_\alpha=d+\dim E_\alpha$).  Poincar\'e duality gives a canonical\footnote{For the moment, we ignore the necessary twist by the orientation sheaf.} identification $\check H^\bullet(X)=H_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)$, which gives the first equality in \eqref{singlechartFC} (this is a rather strong version of Poincar\'e duality, valid for any compact subset $X$ of a manifold $X_\alpha$; we will say more about how to prove it in \S\ref{homotopysheavesintrosec}).  We think of the composite of the maps in \eqref{singlechartFC} as an element $[X]_A^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\check H^d(X)^\vee$, which we call the virtual fundamental class.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart

nodes.name: Single-chart virtual fundamental class diagram
nodes.statement: \check H^d(X)=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}\mathbb Z
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.label: singlechartFC

nodes.name: Algebraic and perturbative virtual classes agree for one chart
assumptions: when $X_\alpha$ has a smooth structure
conclusions: it gives the same answer as the perturbation approach
nodes.statement: The algebraic approach is more general (it does not require a smooth structure on $X_\alpha$), and it is easy to see that it gives the same answer as the perturbation approach when $X_\alpha$ has a smooth structure.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart

nodes.name: Virtual class of $x^n$ and $z^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X=\{0\}$, $X_\alpha=E_\alpha=\mathbb R$, and $s_\alpha(x)=x^n$ ($n\geq 1$). The reader may easily check that with our definition, the virtual fundamental class is $1$ if $n$ is odd and $0$ if $n$ is even (as is consistent with the perturbation picture). Let $X=\{0\}$, $X_\alpha=E_\alpha=\mathbb C$ (considered as an $\mathbb R$-vector space), and $s_\alpha(z)=z^n$ ($n\geq 1$). The reader may check that in this case, the virtual fundamental class is $n$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.statement_short: For $s(x)=x^n$ on $\mathbb R$ the virtual class is $n$ mod 2 (1 or 0); for $s(z)=z^n$ on $\mathbb C$ it is $n$.

nodes.name: Single-chart implicit atlas with covering group
nodes.statement: We have a space $X$, and the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of the following data.  We have a topological manifold $X_\alpha$ (not necessarily compact), a vector space $E_\alpha$, and a continuous function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$.  We have a finite group $\Gamma_\alpha$ acting on $X_\alpha$ and (linearly) on $E_\alpha$ so that $s_\alpha$ is $\Gamma_\alpha$-equivariant.  Finally, we have an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)/\Gamma_\alpha$.  We must now work over the coefficient ring $R=\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma_\alpha}]$.
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class from a single chart with covering group
nodes.statement_short: With covering group $\Gamma_\alpha$, take $\Gamma_\alpha$-invariants of the single-chart diagram and precompose with $\frac1{\#\Gamma_\alpha}$ times pullback.
nodes.statement:
To define the virtual fundamental class we consider:
\begin{equation} \check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0;R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}R
\end{equation}
Now it is a general property of \v Cech cohomology that $\check H^\bullet(Y;R)^\Gamma=\check H^\bullet(Y/\Gamma;R)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $Y$ acted on by a finite group $\Gamma$ as long as $R$ is a module over $\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma}]$.  We precompose \eqref{singlechartisotropyFC} with the canonical isomorphism $\check H^d(X;R)\to\check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}$ given as $\frac 1{\#\Gamma_\alpha}$ times the pullback.  This gives an element $[X]_A^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\check H^d(X;R)^\vee$, which we call the virtual fundamental class.
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)

nodes.name: Single-chart virtual fundamental class with covering group
nodes.statement: \check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0;R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}R
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)
nodes.label: singlechartisotropyFC

nodes.name: \v Cech cohomology of a finite quotient
assumptions: for a compact Hausdorff space $Y$ acted on by a finite group $\Gamma$
as long as $R$ is a module over $\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma}]$
conclusions: $\check H^\bullet(Y;R)^\Gamma=\check H^\bullet(Y/\Gamma;R)$
nodes.statement: Now it is a general property of \v Cech cohomology that $\check H^\bullet(Y;R)^\Gamma=\check H^\bullet(Y/\Gamma;R)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $Y$ acted on by a finite group $\Gamma$ as long as $R$ is a module over $\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma}]$.
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)

nodes.name: Two-chart implicit atlas
nodes.statement:
Our space is $X$, and the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha,\beta\}$ amounts to the following data:
\begin{align}
s_\alpha:X_\alpha&\to E_\alpha&s_\alpha^{-1}(0)=U_\alpha\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\
s_\beta:X_\beta&\to E_\beta&s_\beta^{-1}(0)=U_\beta\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\
s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta:X_{\alpha\beta}&\to E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta&(s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta)^{-1}(0)=U_{\alpha\beta}=U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\subseteq X
\end{align}
which fit together as outlined in \S\ref{protoimplicitatlassection} (and as illustrated in Figure \ref{implicitatlaspicture}\subref{picb}).
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Two-chart implicit atlas data
nodes.statement: s_\alpha:X_\alpha&\to E_\alpha&s_\alpha^{-1}(0)=U_\alpha\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\ s_\beta:X_\beta&\to E_\beta&s_\beta^{-1}(0)=U_\beta\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\ s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta:X_{\alpha\beta}&\to E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta&(s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta)^{-1}(0)=U_{\alpha\beta}=U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\subseteq X
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Virtual cochain complex (term)
nodes.statement: This complex we construct will be called the \emph{virtual cochain complex}.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Local virtual fundamental cycle
nodes.statement: The complex $C_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)$ calculates $\check H^\bullet_c(U_\alpha)$, and the map $s_\ast:C_\bullet(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)\to C_\bullet(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)$ should be thought of as the chain level ``local virtual fundamental cycle'' $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\check H^{\dim X_\alpha-\dim E_\alpha}_c(U_\alpha)^\vee$, which we would like to glue together into the global virtual fundamental cycle.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.statement_short: The single-chart complex computes compactly supported \v Cech cohomology of $U_\alpha$ and $s_\ast$ is the chain-level local virtual fundamental cycle.

nodes.name: Functoriality of virtual cochain complexes
nodes.statement: Technically speaking, it is very important to have a uniform functorial definition of the virtual cochain complexes (one which does not require making any extra choices).
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Mapping cone (first try)
nodes.statement: C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta})\xrightarrow{\cap[s_\beta^{-1}(0)]\oplus\cap[s_\alpha^{-1}(0)]}\begin{matrix}C_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_\beta-\bullet}(X_\beta,X_\beta\setminus U_\beta)\end{matrix}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: mappingconefirsttry

nodes.name: Equation
nodes.statement: C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,[X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha]\times E_\beta)\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times[X_\beta\setminus U_\beta])\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta})
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Strong tubular neighborhood diagrams
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{s_\alpha\oplus\operatorname{id}}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd} \qquad \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{\operatorname{id}\oplus s_\beta}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: strongtubularneighborhood

nodes.name: Deformation to the normal cone
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Deformation to the normal cone $Y_{\alpha\beta}$
nodes.statement: Y_{\alpha\beta}:=\left\{(e_\alpha,e_\beta,t,x)\in E_\alpha\times E_\beta\times[0,1]\times X_{\alpha\beta}\;\middle|\;\begin{matrix}s_\alpha(x)=t\cdot e_\alpha\hfill\cr s_\beta(x)=(1-t)\cdot e_\beta\hfill\end{matrix}\right\}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Fibers of the deformation to the normal cone
nodes.statement_short: $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ is $X_{\alpha\beta}\times(0,1)$ over $(0,1)$, with normal-cone fibers $E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}$, $U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta$ at the ends; it is a manifold by the submersion axiom.
nodes.statement: We think of $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ as a family of spaces parameterized by $[0,1]$ (via the projection $Y_{\alpha\beta}\to[0,1]$).  Observe that if $t\in(0,1)$, then $e_\alpha,e_\beta$ are determined uniquely by $x$.  Therefore, over the open interval $(0,1)$, we see that $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ is a trivial product space $X_{\alpha\beta}\times(0,1)$.  Over the point $t=0$, though, the fiber is $E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}$, which is the ``normal cone'' of the submanifold $U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\subseteq X_{\alpha\beta}$ cut out (transversally!) by the equation $s_\alpha=0$.  Similarly, over the point $t=1$, the fiber is $U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta$.  Also observe that $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ is a manifold by the submersion axiom.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Two-chart virtual cochain complex
nodes.statement_short: For two charts, the virtual cochain complex is the mapping cone of pushforwards from normal-cone chain complexes into chains on $X_\alpha\times E_\beta$, $Y_{\alpha\beta}$, $E_\alpha\times X_\beta$.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Two-chart virtual cochain complex mapping cone
nodes.statement: \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta,U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta},E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix} \to \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,X_\alpha\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(Y_{\alpha\beta},Y_{\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times[0,1]\times U_{\alpha\beta})\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times X_\beta\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: multichartcomplex

nodes.name: Pushforward maps of the two-chart complex
nodes.statement: U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow X_\alpha\times E_\beta\\ U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=1$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=0$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow E_\alpha\times X_\beta
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Virtual Poincar\'e duality isomorphism
nodes.statement: H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)=\check H^\bullet(X)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles
nodes.label: homotopyisogoal

nodes.name: The $\mathcal K$-presheaf $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)=C_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus K)$
nodes.statement: Fix a closed manifold $M$ of dimension $n$.  For any compact subset $K\subseteq M$, let $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)$ denote the complex $C_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus K)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: $\mathcal K$-presheaf of complexes
nodes.statement: This object $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a \emph{$\mathcal K$-presheaf\footnote{The prefix ``$\mathcal K$-'' indicates sections are given over compact sets instead of open sets.  For technical reasons, it is more convenient to work with $\mathcal K$-presheaves rather than presheaves, though at the conceptual level, the reader may safely ignore the difference.} of complexes} (or \emph{complex of $\mathcal K$-presheaves}) on $M$, which just means that we have natural maps $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K')$ for $K\supseteq K'$, which are suitably compatible with each other.
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Sheaf-theoretic proof sketch of Poincar\'e duality
nodes.statement_short: $C_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus K)$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf (Mayer--Vietoris, local homology) with $H^0=\mathfrak o_M$, so \v Cech cohomology computes it.
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Mayer--Vietoris double complex
nodes.statement: \mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cup K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1)\oplus\mathcal F^\bullet(K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cap K_2)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Poincar\'e duality for compact subsets
nodes.statement: H_{n-i}(M,M\setminus K)=H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K)=\check H^i(K;\mathfrak o_M)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles
nodes.label: PDintropurehomotopysheafex

nodes.name: Sketch of the virtual Poincar\'e duality isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: The two-chart complex is the global sections of a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf; a degenerate spectral sequence shows it is pure with known $H^0$, giving $H_{\mathrm{vir}}=\check H$.
nodes.statement: This argument generalizes as follows to prove the isomorphism \eqref{homotopyisogoal}.  For sake of concreteness, let us take $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)$ to be the mapping cone of \eqref{multichartcomplex}, though the general case is not much different.  First of all, we observe that there is a natural complex of $\mathcal K$-presheaves $\mathcal F^\bullet$ on $X$ whose complex of global sections is $C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)$.  Namely, to get $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)$ we simply replace every occurence of $U_\alpha$, $U_\beta$, or $U_{\alpha\beta}$ in \eqref{multichartcomplex} by its intersection with $K$.  Now $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf (extensions of homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves are homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves by Lemma \ref{associatedgradedhomotopysheaf}, and each of the individual complexes appearing in \eqref{multichartcomplex} gives a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf by Mayer--Vietoris).  To prove that $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is pure and to identify its $H^0$, we can calculate $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(\{p\})$ using a spectral sequence which degenerates at the $E_2$ term (this is the argument in Lemma \ref{gluingcechsimple}).  It is this second step where it matters that we glued the complexes together ``correctly''.  Since $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf and we have identified its $H^0$, this gives the desired isomorphism.
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Concatenation map of Floer moduli spaces
nodes.statement: \overline{\mathcal M}(p,q)\times\overline{\mathcal M}(q,r)\to\overline{\mathcal M}(p,r)
nodes.label: concatintro

nodes.name: Implicit atlas with boundary (informal)
nodes.statement: Such an atlas on a space $X$ is given by the same data as an implicit atlas, except that in addition we specify closed subsets $\partial X_I\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$ which are compatible with the $\psi_{IJ}$, and we modify the transversality axioms to assert that $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a manifold with boundary $\partial X_I\cap X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$.

nodes.name: Product implicit atlas (observation)
assumptions: implicit atlases $A$ on $X$ and $A'$ on $X'$
conclusions: induce an implicit atlas $A\sqcup A'$ (disjoint union of index sets) on $X\times X'$
nodes.statement: This is a special case of a general observation: implicit atlases $A$ on $X$ and $A'$ on $X'$ induce an implicit atlas $A\sqcup A'$ (disjoint union of index sets) on $X\times X'$, simply by defining $(X\times X')_{I\sqcup I'}:=X_I\times X'_{I'}$.

nodes.name: Restriction of an implicit atlas to the boundary
assumptions: an implicit atlas with boundary on $X$
conclusions: induces an implicit atlas (with the same index set) on $\partial X$
nodes.statement: This is also a special case of a general observation: an implicit atlas with boundary on $X$ induces an implicit atlas (with the same index set) on $\partial X$, simply by defining $(\partial X)_I:=\partial X_I$.

nodes.name: Compatibility of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: Now, a good notion of ``compatibility'' between two implicit atlases $A$ and $B$ on a space $X$ is the existence of an implicit atlas on $X$ with index set $A\sqcup B$, whose subatlases $A$ and $B$ coincide with the given atlases.

nodes.name: No canonical union of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: In theory, there is no way to go from a pair of implicit atlases $A$ and $B$ on a space $X$ to an implicit atlas $A\sqcup B$ on $X$ whose subatlases $A$ and $B$ coincide with the given atlases (and there is no uniqueness for atlases $A\sqcup B$ with this property). However in practice, there is often a natural choice of such an atlas, which moreover is essentially the only reasonable choice. The atlas (\ref{IAPQR}) is a good example of this.
nodes.statement_short: Two implicit atlases need not admit a combined atlas $A\sqcup B$, but in practice a natural choice exists, e.g. the atlas (IAPQR).

nodes.name: Set of generators
nodes.statement: We fix a finite set $\mathcal P$ (the ``set of generators'') equipped with partial order $\prec$ and a grading $\operatorname{gr}:\mathcal P\to\mathbb Z$.

nodes.name: Spaces of broken trajectories and concatenation maps
nodes.statement:
For all pairs $p\prec q$ in $\mathcal P$, we fix a compact Hausdorff space $\mathcal X(p,q)$ (the ``space of broken trajectories from $p$ to $q$'').  These spaces $\mathcal X(p,q)$ are also equipped with ``concatenation maps'':
\begin{equation} \mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)\to\mathcal X(p,r)
\end{equation}
which satisfy some natural properties, in particular associativity.

nodes.name: Concatenation maps of a flow category
nodes.statement: \mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)\to\mathcal X(p,r)
nodes.label: productmapexample

nodes.name: Flow category
nodes.statement: We call such a pair $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$ (when defined precisely) a \emph{flow category}.

nodes.name: Morse--Smale flow category
differentia: every $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is a manifold with corners of dimension $\operatorname{gr}(q)-\operatorname{gr}(p)-1$ in a manner compatible with the concatenation maps \eqref{productmapexample}
nodes.statement: This terminology is due to Cohen--Jones--Segal \cite{cohenjonessegal}, who used it to mean something closer to what we prefer to call a \emph{Morse--Smale flow category}, namely a flow category in which every $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is a manifold with corners of dimension $\operatorname{gr}(q)-\operatorname{gr}(p)-1$ in a manner compatible with the concatenation maps \eqref{productmapexample}.

nodes.name: Flow category of a Morse function
nodes.statement: The basic example of a flow category is the flow category of a Morse function: $\mathcal P$ is the set of critical points, and $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is the space of (broken) Morse trajectories from $p$ to $q$; if the Morse function is Morse--Smale, then this flow category is Morse--Smale.

nodes.name: Morse complex of a Morse--Smale flow category
assumptions: Given a Morse--Smale flow category $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$
conclusions: one can construct a map $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ by counting those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $0$
one can prove that $d^2=0$ by considering those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $1$
nodes.statement: Given a Morse--Smale flow category $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$, one can construct a map $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ by counting those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $0$, and one can prove that $d^2=0$ by considering those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $1$.

nodes.name: Choice of compatible system of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: There are many different choices for what one could mean by a ``compatible system of implicit atlases'' $\mathcal A(p,q)$ on the spaces $\mathcal X(p,q)$. For sake of exposition, we have chosen here the structure for which it is \emph{easiest to apply the VFC package}. In the actual construction in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}, we use the structure which is the \emph{easiest to construct in practice} (via the natural generalization of \S\ref{floerintroIA}). As a result, various complexes that here \emph{coincide} are only \emph{canonically quasi-isomorphic} in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}. Basically, this means that in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}, we will have to take lots of homotopy colimits to make certain maps well-defined on the chain level. A systematic use of $\infty$-categories of complexes would tame the resulting explosion of notation, at the cost of relying on that more abstract language/machinery.
nodes.statement_short: The introduction uses the compatible structure easiest for applying the VFC package; Section 7 uses the one easiest to construct, needing homotopy colimits.

nodes.name: Coboundary map from the boundary
nodes.statement: C_{\mathrm{vir}}^{\bullet-1}(\partial X)\to C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)
nodes.label: introcoboundary

nodes.name: Isomorphism $H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X)=\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_X)$
nodes.statement: H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_X)
nodes.label: HXisointro

nodes.name: Isomorphism $H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)=\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial})$
nodes.statement: H^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial})
nodes.label: HXrelisointro

nodes.name: Map $s_\ast$ to chains on $E_A$
nodes.statement: C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)\xrightarrow{s_\ast}C_{\dim E_A-\bullet}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)
nodes.label: thomintro

nodes.name: Product map on virtual cochain complexes
nodes.statement: C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet([\mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)]\operatorname{rel}\partial)

nodes.name: Product map to the boundary
nodes.statement: C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))
nodes.label: productmapfromIA

nodes.name: Compatibility of product maps with $s_\ast$
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\ar{r}{\eqref{productmapfromIA}}\ar{d}{s_\ast\otimes s_\ast}&C_{\mathrm{vir}}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))\ar{d}{s_\ast}\\ C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0) \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: productofVCandonEcompare

nodes.name: Chain level coherent orientations and Thom cocycles
nodes.statement_short: Choices defining $d$: cochains $\lambda(p,q)$ with $d\lambda=\mu$ inducing the given orientation, and compatible Thom cocycles $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\mu(p,r)$
nodes.statement: \mu(p,r):=\sum_{p\prec q\prec r}\lambda(p,q)\cdot\lambda(q,r)\in C_{\mathrm{vir}}^0(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))
nodes.label: boundarychainlevelcoherent

nodes.name: Compatibility of Thom cocycles
nodes.statement: \hspace{-1.5cm} \begin{tikzcd} C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]\otimes[[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]]}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd} \hspace{-1.5cm}
nodes.label: coherentcofundamentalcocycles

nodes.name: Boundary operator $d$ from coherent choices
nodes.definiendum: boundary operator $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$
nodes.statement: Given such choices, we define the boundary operator $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ to have ``matrix coefficients'' $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]](s_\ast\lambda(p,q))$.

nodes.name: $d^2=0$ for the virtual Floer differential
nodes.statement: One can show that $d^2=0$ by using $d\lambda(p,q)=\mu(p,q)$ and the compatibilities \eqref{productofVCandonEcompare} and \eqref{coherentcofundamentalcocycles}.

nodes.name: Sketch of existence of coherent choices $\lambda$, $[[E]]$
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $(p,q)$: $\lambda$ exists since the class of $\mu$ can be checked locally (sheaf property, stratification); $[[E]]$ needs cofibrant replacements.

nodes.name: Compatibility diagram on homology
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]\otimes[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]\mapsto 1}&H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]\mapsto 1}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: coherentcofundamentalcocycleshomology

nodes.name: Sketch of independence of choices
nodes.statement_short: Independence of $(\lambda,[[E]])$ via an inductively constructed chain map between the resulting complexes.
nodes.statement: Finally, we should argue that the homology groups defined via a choice of $(\lambda,[[E]])$ are in fact independent of that choice.  For this, we use the usual strategy of constructing a chain map between $(\mathbb Z[\mathcal P],d)$ and $(\mathbb Z[\mathcal P],d')$ for any $d$ and $d'$ arising from $(\lambda,[[E]])$ and $(\lambda',[[E]]')$ respectively (plus appropriate chain homotopies).  To construct such a chain map, we use a similar inductive procedure, starting from the base choices $(\lambda,[[E]])$ and $(\lambda',[[E]]')$.  Note that for this argument for independence of choice to work, the inductive nature of our construction is crucial.

nodes.name: $S^1$-equivariant implicit atlas (informal)
nodes.statement: The most basic setting in which our results apply (and are interesting) is that of a free $S^1$-space $X$ (i.e.\ a space with a free action of $S^1$) equipped with an $S^1$-equivariant implicit atlas $A$.  Such an atlas is simply an implicit atlas where all the thickenings $X_I$ are equipped with an action of $S^1$ so that the functions $\psi_{IJ}$ are $S^1$-equivariant and the functions $s_I$ are $S^1$-invariant.

nodes.name: $S^1$-localization (free action)
assumptions: In the above setup
conclusions: $\pi_\ast[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$
if the virtual dimension $d$ of $X$ is zero, then $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$
nodes.statement_short: For a free $S^1$-space with $S^1$-equivariant implicit atlas, the virtual class pushes forward to zero on $X/S^1$; in dimension zero it vanishes.
nodes.statement: In the above setup, our $S^1$-localization result states that $\pi_\ast[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$, where $\pi:X\to X/S^1$ is the quotient map and $\pi_\ast:\check H^\bullet(X)^\vee\to\check H^\bullet(X/S^1)^\vee$ is the dual of the pullback $\pi^\ast:\check H^\bullet(X/S^1)\to\check H^\bullet(X)$.  Observe that $\pi_\ast$ is an isomorphism for $\bullet=0$ (since $S^1$ is connected), hence this implies that if the virtual dimension $d$ of $X$ is zero, then $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$.

nodes.name: Quotient implicit atlas on $X/S^1$ need not exist
nodes.statement: A natural strategy for proving $S^1$-localization results is to consider $X_I/S^1$ as forming an atlas on $X/S^1$ of virtual dimension one less, and then ``pulling back'' to $X$ the virtual fundamental cycle on $X/S^1$ (this is the approach taken by Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{fukayaono,foootechnicaldetails}). In the general setting where the $S^1$-action is merely continuous, the implicit atlas on $X$ does not induce an implicit atlas on $X/S^1$ because of the existence of free $S^1$-actions on topological manifolds whose quotients are not manifolds\footnote{Such an action may be constructed out of any non-manifold $X$ for which $X\times\mathbb R$ is a manfold (namely the obvious action on $X\times S^1$). Many examples of such spaces are known, the first being due to Bing \cite{bingstablemanifoldexample}; see also Cannon \cite{cannon}.}, though we still consider this ``quotient implicit atlas'' in spirit. This extra generality is convenient, since it means we do not need to construct an $S^1$-equivariant gluing map (providing the local slice necessary to show that the ``quotient implicit atlas'' exists).
nodes.statement_short: For merely continuous free $S^1$-actions the quotient $X_I/S^1$ need not be a manifold, so the FOOO quotient-atlas strategy is unavailable; avoided here.
nodes.label: cannotquotientbySS

nodes.name: Proof of $S^1$-localization for a single chart
nodes.statement_short: Compare the single-chart diagram with its $S^1$-equivariant version via Gysin maps $\pi^!$; the right $\pi^!$ vanishes as $S^1$ acts trivially on $E_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Single equivariant chart
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a single $S^1$-equivariant chart.
nodes.statement: Let us now prove our assertion $\pi_\ast[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$ in the simple case of a single chart (for which we defined $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}$ in \S\ref{vfcsinglechart}).  In this case, the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of a topological manifold $X_\alpha$, a function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$, and an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)$.  This atlas being $S^1$-equivariant means that $X_\alpha$ is equipped with an $S^1$-action for which $s_\alpha$ is $S^1$-invariant and which induces the given action on $X$.

nodes.name: Comparison diagram
nodes.statement_short: Display the diagram comparing equivariant and ordinary single-chart virtual classes.

nodes.name: Vertical maps
nodes.statement_short: Identify vertical maps as pullback and Gysin maps $\pi^!$.

nodes.name: Gysin long exact sequence
nodes.statement: \cdots\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}H_\bullet(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi_\ast}H_\bullet^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-2}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}\cdots

nodes.name: Equivariant Poincare duality
nodes.statement_short: Horizontal identifications are Poincar\'e duality, using freeness of the action.
nodes.statement: The two leftmost horizontal identifications are a form of Poincar\'e duality (which can be proven, along with the commutativity of the square, with homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves as in \S\ref{homotopysheavesintrosec}); it is at this step where we use the fact that $S^1$ acts freely on $X$.

nodes.name: Right Gysin map vanishes
nodes.statement_short: The rightmost $\pi^!$ vanishes since $S^1$ acts trivially on $E_\alpha$; conclude.
nodes.statement: Now $[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}$ is by definition the composition of the bottom row.  Hence $\pi_\ast[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}$ is the map from the upper left corner to the bottom right.  On the other hand, the rightmost vertical map $\pi^!:H_{\dim E_\alpha-1}^{S^1}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\to H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)$ vanishes since $S^1$ acts trivially on $E_\alpha$.  It follows that $\pi_\ast[X]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0$ as desired.

nodes.name: $S^1$-equivariant virtual cochain complexes (informal)
nodes.statement: To define the $S^1$-equivariant virtual cochain complexes, we use the same definition as for the ordinary virtual cochain complexes, except using (shifted) $S^1$-equivariant chains $C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}$ in place of chains $C_\bullet$.

nodes.name: No $S^1$-equivariant virtual fundamental class constructed
nodes.statement: We do not construct an $S^1$-equivariant virtual fundamental class, nor do we address $S^1$-localization for actions which are not free or almost free (having finite stabilizer at every point). However, the machinery we develop could potentially be used for these purposes, see Remark \ref{SSequivariantvfcmaybe}.

nodes.name: Implicit atlas
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. An \emph{implicit atlas of dimension $d=\operatorname{vdim}_AX$} on $X$ is an index set $A$ along with the following data: \begin{rlist} \item(Covering groups) A finite group $\Gamma_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in A$ (let $\Gamma_I:=\prod_{\alpha\in I}\Gamma_\alpha$). \item(Obstruction spaces) A finitely generated $\mathbb R[\Gamma_\alpha]$-module $E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in A$ (let $E_I:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$). \item(Thickenings) A Hausdorff $\Gamma_I$-space $X_I$ for all finite $I\subseteq A$, and a homeomorphism $X\to X_\varnothing$. \item(Kuranishi maps) A $\Gamma_\alpha$-equivariant function $s_\alpha:X_I\to E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in I\subseteq A$ (for $I\subseteq J$, let $s_I:X_J\to E_I$ denote $\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}s_\alpha$). \item(Footprints) A $\Gamma_I$-invariant open set $U_{IJ}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \item(Footprint maps) A $\Gamma_J$-equivariant function $\psi_{IJ}:(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)\to U_{IJ}$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \item(Regular locus) A $\Gamma_I$-invariant subset $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$. \end{rlist} which must satisfy the following ``compatibility axioms'': \begin{rlist} \item$\psi_{IJ}\psi_{JK}=\psi_{IK}$ and $\psi_{II}=\operatorname{id}$. \item$s_I\psi_{IJ}=s_I$. \item$U_{IJ_1}\cap U_{IJ_2}=U_{I,J_1\cup J_2}$ and $U_{II}=X_I$. \item$\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(U_{IK})=U_{JK}\cap(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)$.\footnote{Added in proof: Abouzaid recently pointed out that this axiom is superfluous; it is implied by the other axioms.} \item(Homeomorphism axiom) $\psi_{IJ}$ induces a homeomorphism $(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)/\Gamma_{J\setminus I}\to U_{IJ}$. \setcounter{rcountsave}{\value{rcounti}} \end{rlist} and the following ``transversality axioms'': \begin{rlist} \setcounter{rcounti}{\value{rcountsave}} \item$\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})\subseteq X_J^{\mathrm{reg}}$. \item$\Gamma_{J\setminus I}$ acts freely on $\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})$. \item(Openness axiom) $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_I$ is open. \item(Submersion axiom) The map $s_{J\setminus I}:X_J\to E_{J\setminus I}$ is locally modeled on the projection $\mathbb R^{d+\dim E_I}\times\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}\to\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}$ over $\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})\subseteq X_J$. \item(Covering axiom) $X_\varnothing=\bigcup_{I\subseteq A}\psi_{\varnothing I}((s_I|X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})^{-1}(0))$. \end{rlist}
nodes.genus: an index set $A$ along with the following data
nodes.statement_short: An implicit atlas on compact Hausdorff $X$: covering groups, obstruction spaces, thickenings, Kuranishi maps, footprints and footprint maps, regular loci, satisfying compatibility and transversality axioms.
nodes.label: implicitatlasdefinition

nodes.name: Weakening of implicit atlas axioms
nodes.statement: The VFC machinery in this paper would go through admitting a slight weakening of the axioms of an implicit atlas. For example, we only ever use the fact that the openness and submersion axioms hold in a neighborhood of $(s_I|X_I)^{-1}(0)$. We will not make this precise here, however, since the constructions of implicit atlases we know of would not be made any easier by such a weakening of the axioms.

nodes.name: Smooth implicit atlas
nodes.statement: A \emph{smooth structure} on an implicit atlas consists of a smooth structure on each $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$ such that: \begin{rlist} \item$\Gamma_I$ acts smoothly on $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$. \item$s_I$ is smooth over $X_I^{\mathrm{reg}}$. \item$s_{J\setminus I}:X_J\to E_{J\setminus I}$ is a smooth submersion over $\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})$. \item$\psi_{IJ}$ is a local diffeomorphism over $\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(X_I^{\mathrm{reg}})$. \end{rlist}
nodes.label: smoothIAdef

nodes.name: Smoothness not needed for VFC machinery
nodes.statement: The VFC machinery in this paper applies to implicit atlases (without a smooth structure), though the notion of a smooth implicit atlas may be useful for other applications of implicit atlases.

nodes.name: Using finite $I\to A$ instead of finite $I\subseteq A$
nodes.statement: An implicit atlas consists of data parameterized by the \emph{category of finite subsets of $A$} (objects: finite subsets, morphisms: inclusions). A direct modification of the definition allows one to instead use the \emph{category of finite sets over $A$} (objects: finite sets $I\to A$, morphisms: injective maps $I\hookrightarrow J$ compatible with the maps to $A$). In fact, all constructions of implicit atlases we know of yield implicit atlases in this generalized sense. We won't need this generalization in this paper, but let us point out some reasons why it may be useful to keep in mind. With the definition as it stands now (using finite subsets of $A$), we can ``pull back'' an implicit atlas along any \emph{injection} $B\hookrightarrow A$. If we instead use finite sets over $A$, then we can pull back an implicit atlas along any \emph{map} $B\to A$ (in fact, we can pull back along any \emph{coproduct preserving functor} from finite sets over $B$ to finite sets over $A$, which amounts to the specification of a finite set $I_\beta\to A$ for all $\beta\in B$). Also, in the category of finite subsets of $A$ we can only take the disjoint union of subsets which are already disjoint; however in the category of finite sets over $A$ there exist arbitrary abstract finite disjoint unions. This allows some extra (though currently unneeded) flexibility in certain constructions, since we do not need to ensure certain sets are disjoint or that certain maps are injective. Using the category of sets over $A$ is also the natural perspective to take if we wanted to allow $A$ to be a groupoid instead of a set (then an object is a finite set $I$ along with a collection of objects $\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $A$, and a morphism $(I,\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I})\to(J,\{\alpha_j\}_{j\in J})$ is an injection $j:I\hookrightarrow J$ along with isomorphisms $\alpha_i\xrightarrow\sim\alpha_{j(i)}$ in $A$).
nodes.statement_short: Implicit atlases may be indexed by finite sets over $A$ rather than subsets, allowing pullback along arbitrary maps, abstract disjoint unions and groupoid index sets.
nodes.label: bettertouseovercategory

nodes.name: Implicit atlas with boundary
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space together with a closed subset denoted $\partial X\subseteq X$. An \emph{implicit atlas of dimension $d$ with boundary} on $X$ consists of the same data as an implicit atlas, except that in addition we specify a $\Gamma_I$-invariant closed subset $\partial X_I\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$, such that $\partial X_\varnothing=\partial X$. We add the following ``compatibility axiom'': \begin{rlist} \item$\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(\partial X_I)=(s_{J\setminus I}|\partial X_J)^{-1}(0)$. \setcounter{rcountsave}{\value{rcounti}} \end{rlist} and we modify one ``transversality axiom'': \begin{rlist} \setcounter{rcounti}{\value{rcountsave}} \item(Submersion axiom) We allow an additional local model $\mathbb R_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb R^{d+\dim E_I-1}\times\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}\to\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}$, and $\partial X_J^{\mathrm{reg}}\subseteq X_J^{\mathrm{reg}}$ must correspond to the boundary of the local model. \end{rlist}
nodes.definiendum: implicit atlas of dimension $d$ with boundary
nodes.statement_short: Implicit atlas on $(X,\partial X)$: adds invariant closed boundary subsets $\partial X_I$ compatible with footprint maps, and a boundary local model in the submersion axiom.
nodes.label: IAwboundary

nodes.name: Implicit atlas as special case of implicit atlas with boundary
nodes.statement: Just as a manifold is a special case of a manifold with boundary, an implicit atlas is a special case of an implicit atlas with boundary (namely where $\partial X_I=\varnothing$ for all $I$).

nodes.name: Restriction of implicit atlas to boundary
